extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/prosecutors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claims, claim amendments, or specification amendments satisfy the written description requirement and whether amendments introduce prohibited new matter under U.S. law (35 U.S.C. §§112, 119, 120, 132, 251). Intended to direct examiner practice and prosecution strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims/support must be supported by the description as filed
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new claim or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed; amendments to the specification (e.g., change in the definition of a term used both in the specification and claim) may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim or claim amendment is not supported by the originally filed description, it may introduce new matter and be improper. Examiners should examine specification changes for indirect effects on claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on parent filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 requires 112(a) support
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of the filing date of an earlier U.S. application only if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) in the earlier-filed application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting priority to a parent U.S. application under 35 U.S.C. 120, ensure that each claimed subject matter is supported by the parent disclosure as required by written description law. See Tronzo v. Biomet, In re Scheiber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on foreign/provisional priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 requires 112(a) support
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application can obtain benefit of a foreign priority date or provisional filing date only if the corresponding earlier application supports the claims in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not grant priority based solely on filing dates; substantively compare claim subject matter to the earlier disclosure for written description support. See In re Ziegler, Kawai v. Metlesics, In re Gosteli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for a claim corresponding to an interference count
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim corresponding to a count in an interference must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a party seeks benefit of an earlier-filed U.S. application for an interference count, the earlier application must meet 112(a) for the subject matter of the count. Broad generic disclosure to a class is insufficient for a specific compound. See Fields v. Conover, Hyatt v. Boone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claim possibly lacking written description (functional claiming / genus-species gap)
rubrics_metrics.description: An original claim may lack written description support when (1) the claim defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved; or (2) a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence that the genus is contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere presence of claim language in the specification is not dispositive; the specification must describe the claimed invention so one skilled in the art can recognize what is claimed. See Ariad Pharm. v. Eli Lilly and Enzo Biochem v. Gen-Probe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-(or step-)plus-function limitations and indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: A means- or step-plus-function limitation is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents. If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts that perform the entire claimed function, the limitation is indefinite (failure to particularly point out and distinctly claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of corresponding structure makes the claim indefinite and also can fail the written description requirement because an unbounded functional limitation covers all ways of performing a function, indicating lack of possession. See In re Donaldson Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the examiner regarding written description (presumption and rebuttal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification as filed is presumed to provide an adequate written description unless and until the examiner presents sufficient evidence or reasoning to rebut the presumption; the inquiry is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the claimed invention. See In re Wertheim, In re Marzocchi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement-of-rejection requirements for lack of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which support the conclusion: (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general allegation (e.g., 'unpredictability in the art') is insufficient. A simple statement pointing to absence of support for the limitation may be sufficient for new/amended claims. Where appropriate, suggest claim amendments supported by the original disclosure but avoid adding new matter. See MPEP §2163 and Hyatt v. Dudas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner treatment of applicant reply to written-description rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply, the examiner must review the basis for the rejection in view of the record as a whole (including amendments, arguments, and evidence). If the record demonstrates written description is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection; if not, fully respond and properly treat applicant's showings and affidavits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before repeating a 35 U.S.C. 112(a) rejection, re-evaluate the whole record. If maintained, thoroughly analyze affidavits or other evidence submitted in reply. See In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to claim scope after filing require original support (broadening/narrowing/range/terminology changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to meet the written description requirement commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow claim breadth, alter a numerical range limitation, or use claim language not synonymous with terminology used in the original disclosure. Each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure to comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or to be entitled to earlier priority dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing amended claims or claims in a child application seeking priority, check whether each limitation has clear support in the original disclosure. See MPEP §2163.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening by omission of a limitation (omitting an essential/critical element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention. A claim that omits an element which the applicant describes as an essential or critical feature of the original disclosure does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for express statements in the specification that a feature is 'the only possible location' or 'essential' to the invention; omitting such features can cause rejection. Compare cases such as Gentry Gallery, Tronzo, In re Wilder, In re Sus, In re Peters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of a generic (genus) claim requires sufficient species disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported through sufficient description of a representative number of species; when there is substantial variation within the genus, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation. A single species may support a genus only if the disclosure indicates the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether disclosed species are representative of the claimed genus; courts have found genus unsupported where only one structurally similar species is described and not representative (see AbbVie v. Janssen, Enzo Biochem, In re Curtis). There are exceptions when one species would reasonably signal a broader genus to skilled artisans (see In re Rasmussen, In re Herschler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim changes must be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing claim changes that narrow the claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violates the written description requirement; subgeneric terminology may or may not be acceptable depending on whether species within the subgenus are disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'laundry list' of possible moieties does not necessarily support each species. Whether a subgenus is described by a genus plus a species depends on whether the skilled artisan would be reasonably led to that subgenus. Each case is fact-specific. See Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, Rozbicki v. Chiang, In re Lukach, Ex parte Sorenson, In re Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing numerical range limitations requires consideration of inherent support
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing numerical range limitations, analysis must consider which ranges one skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure; some range changes (e.g., adding an unbounded 'at least' with no upper limit) may read on embodiments outside the originally disclosed ranges and thus fail written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare original ranges and examples to proposed ranges; a limitation 'between 35% and 60%' may be supported whereas 'at least 35%' with no upper bound may not. See In re Wertheim, Purdue Pharma v. Faulding, Union Oil v. Atlantic Richfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description to new matter (statutory prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of written description generally concerns claim subject matter. If an applicant amends abstract, specification, or drawings to add matter not described in the application as filed, new matter issues arise. Two statutory provisions prohibit introducing new matter: 35 U.S.C. 132 (no amendment shall introduce new matter) and 35 U.S.C. 251 (no new matter in reissue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information present in any one part of the application as filed may be added to another part without introducing new matter, but adding content not present in the filed disclosure is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of new matter by examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure (abstract, specification, drawings), the examiner should object under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 and require applicant to cancel the new matter; if new matter is added to the claims, reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when new matter is added, the examiner should still consider the subject matter in making prior art rejections because the new matter rejection may be overcome by applicant. When specification amended to add new matter, reject claims when any claim limitations are affected by the added material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review procedures for new matter objections and rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection of claims is reviewable by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB), whereas an objection and requirement to delete new matter is subject to supervisory review by petition under 37 CFR 1.181. If both claims and specification contain new matter and there has been both a rejection and an objection, the issue becomes appealable and should not be decided by petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow proper administrative routes: appeals for rejections, petitions for objections; do not conflate procedures when both rejection and objection exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; remedy for claimed subject matter not in remainder of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims filed in the original specification are part of the disclosure. If the original specification contains a claim disclosing material not disclosed in the remainder of the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Form paragraph 7.44 where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification. See In re Benno.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description are not new matter (rephrasing allowed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to an application which are supported in the original description are NOT new matter. Mere rephrasing where the same meaning remains intact is permissible. Inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at filing may generally not be new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple definitions exist and applicant adds a particular definition, the original disclosure must make clear that applicant intended that definition to avoid new matter/lack of written description issues. See In re Anderson, Scarring Corp. v. Megan, Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of obvious errors does not constitute new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would both recognize the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign priority documents of record may not be used to support correction of an error in the pending U.S. application unless the U.S. application explicitly incorporates the foreign document by reference. See In re Odd, Ex parte Bondiou, and rules for incorporation by reference (37 CFR 1.57(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent functions/theory/advantages may be relied on (no new matter introduced)
rubrics_metrics.description: By disclosing a device that inherently performs a function or has a property, or operates according to a theory or has an advantage, the patent application necessarily discloses that function, theory or advantage even though it says nothing explicit concerning it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application may later be amended to recite the inherently disclosed function/theory/advantage without introducing prohibited new matter. See In re Reynolds, In re Smythe.
